strengths: Rigorous and fairly complete theoretical treatment of the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) for classifier neuromanifolds, grounded in a careful spectral analysis of the low-dimensional 'core space' (statistical simplex), including tight eigenvalue bounds (Theorem 1) and Löwner-order bounds (Lemma 2) with matching error analysis (Lemmas 3-5).

Novel and practically appealing random estimator (Hutchinson's estimate) of the full FIM (not just the diagonal) that requires only a single extra backward pass, reuses forward-pass logits, and can target diagonal, block-diagonal, low-rank, or full structure via different scalarizing functions (h, h^DG, h^LR).

Strong theoretical guarantees: the proposed estimator is proven unbiased with a bounded coefficient of variation (CV ≤ √2), in contrast to the empirical FIM (shown to have unbounded worst-case error under adversarial labels, Lemma 4/Proposition 11) and standard Monte Carlo estimators (shown to have unbounded CV via a heavy-tailed counterexample).

Clear connection between the low-dimensional core geometry and the high-dimensional neuromanifold via the pullback/Gauss-Newton relationship (Eq. 4), which is used systematically to lift core-space bounds to deterministic FIM bounds (Propositions 6-11).

Reasonably thorough related-work positioning relative to natural gradient methods, Kronecker-factored approximations, and prior Hutchinson-trace-based Hessian/FIM estimators, clarifying the paper's specific contribution (full-tensor, architecture-agnostic estimator via AD detach tricks).
Proofs are provided in detail in the appendix, aiding reproducibility of the theoretical claims.
weaknesses: Empirical validation is thin: only qualitative density plots of diagonal FIM entries on DistilBERT for two text classification datasets; there is no quantitative comparison against a brute-force/ground-truth FIM to verify the tightness of the proposed bounds or the predicted variance formulas.

No downstream demonstration of practical utility (e.g., natural gradient optimization, pruning, or generalization studies) despite the paper motivating the work via natural gradient and optimization applications in the introduction and related work.
No wall-clock/memory benchmarking comparing the proposed Hutchinson estimator, eFIM, and MC estimator, despite computational efficiency being a central selling point of the method.

Experiments are run on a single CPU (MacBook Pro M1) with a small model (DistilBERT) and small sample sizes (128 examples, 10 Hutchinson samples); it is unclear how the method scales to larger models or how bound tightness behaves for architectures beyond a simple softmax classification head.

The low-rank estimator's reliance on a separately approximated power-iteration for λ_C and v_C introduces an additional source of error that is not incorporated into the paper's variance/CV guarantees.

The contribution, while technically solid, is fairly narrow in scope (single-task classification FIM geometry) and its broader significance/impact for the wider ML community is not strongly established beyond the information-geometry niche.
The presentation is dense and heavily notation-laden; while proofs are deferred to the appendix, the main text could better emphasize practical takeaways and intuition for a broader audience.

strengths: The paper provides a rigorous, self-contained theoretical treatment of the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) spectrum on the low-dimensional statistical simplex ('core space'), including tight eigenvalue bounds (Theorem 1) and Löwner-order bounds (Lemma 2) that are then pulled back to bound the FIM on the full neuromanifold (Proposition 6 and related corollaries).

The proposed Hutchinson-trick-based estimator of the full FIM (not just its trace) is a nice technical contribution: it is unbiased, computable with a single extra backward pass reusing forward-pass logits, and provably has bounded coefficient of variation (CV ≤ √2), in contrast to the empirical FIM and naive Monte Carlo estimators, which the authors show can have unbounded CV/adversarial-case error (Lemmas 4, 5, and Proposition 11).

The theoretical analysis is thorough, with detailed proofs of every claim placed in an extensive appendix, and the paper clearly connects to and positions itself against a substantial body of related work on natural gradient, KFAC, empirical Fisher critiques, and Hutchinson-type estimators.
The estimator is architecture-agnostic and applicable beyond neural networks to general parametric statistical models, which is a nice generality claim.
weaknesses: The empirical validation is very weak: the only experiments are qualitative kernel-density plots of diagonal FIM entries on DistilBERT for two text classification tasks, with no ground-truth comparison, no quantitative error/variance measurements, no wall-clock/computational cost comparisons against baselines (MC, eFIM, KFAC), and no statistical significance testing.

There is no demonstration that the proposed estimator (or the deterministic bounds) provides any practical benefit in a downstream task, e.g., improved natural gradient optimization, better generalization, or faster convergence — this is explicitly deferred to future work, leaving the paper's practical significance largely unproven.

Many of the core technical tools (Cauchy interlacing, Gershgorin circle theorem, Hoffman–Wielandt inequality, Von Neumann trace inequality) are classical, and their application here, while carefully executed, is somewhat incremental rather than introducing fundamentally new analysis techniques.

The paper claims the estimator can be used for 'diagonal, block-diagonal, or full' FIM estimation, but the variance/CV guarantees are only proven and empirically illustrated for diagonal entries; off-diagonal or block-diagonal behavior is not empirically validated.

The numerical simulations use a small number of samples (128 data points, 10 Hutchinson probes) on a single small-to-mid-size model (DistilBERT) without ablations over sample size, probe count, or architecture, limiting generalizability of the empirical observations.
The relationship and quantitative advantage over the closely related prior work of Soen & Sun (2024) on diagonal FIM estimator trade-offs is asserted qualitatively but not empirically benchmarked.

strengths: The paper provides a genuinely novel theoretical decomposition of the FIM problem: analyzing the low-dimensional 'core space' (the statistical simplex) first, then pulling the resulting spectral bounds back to the high-dimensional neuromanifold via the Gauss-Newton/pullback structure. This is an elegant and underexplored strategy.

Theorem 1 and Lemma 2 give tight, interpretable spectral bounds (rank-1 lower bound, diagonal upper bound) for the simplex FIM, with rigorous proofs (Cauchy interlacing, Gershgorin) provided in detail in the appendix.

The proposed Hutchinson-based estimator is a meaningful practical contribution: it is unbiased, computable via a single extra backward pass (reusing forward-pass logits), and — unlike the empirical FIM or naive Monte Carlo estimators — has a provably bounded coefficient of variation (CV ≤ √2), which is a concrete and appealing theoretical guarantee.

The paper carefully diagnoses why existing FIM approximations (eFIM, plain MC) can be arbitrarily bad (Lemma 4, Proposition 11, and the heavy-tailed MC counterexample in Section 4.1), which strengthens the motivation for the proposed estimator.

The work is well positioned relative to related literature (natural gradient, K-FAC, empirical Fisher critiques, MC information geometry, Hutchinson trace/Hessian estimators), with a clear articulation of what is new.
The estimator is architecture-agnostic and applies to any classifier of the form p(y|x,θ), which is a nice generality claim.
Detailed, self-contained proofs are provided for essentially every stated result, supporting reproducibility of the theoretical claims.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is very thin: only qualitative density plots of diagonal FIM entries on two DistilBERT/text-classification setups (AG News, SST-2), with no downstream validation (e.g., plugging the estimator into a natural-gradient-style optimizer, or comparing against K-FAC/other approximations on an actual training or generalization metric).

No quantitative comparison of bound tightness or estimator accuracy against ground truth or other estimators (e.g., relative error, wall-clock time, or convergence of variance with sample count) — the visual density plots alone don't substantiate quantitative superiority.
Computational cost claims ('single backward pass', 'practical for large scale networks') are asserted but not empirically measured (no runtime/memory benchmarks against K-FAC, eFIM, or MC baselines).

The dense and heavily overloaded notation (many near-identical symbols such as I/Î/𝕀, F/F̂/𝔽, superscripts DG/LR/∆) makes the paper hard to follow and could limit accessibility and reproducibility for readers not deeply steeped in information geometry notation.

The practical significance of the tight bounds is not fully demonstrated — e.g., how much does the tighter lower bound (proposition 6/9) versus the looser upper bound actually matter in a concrete downstream use case (optimization, pruning, uncertainty estimation)?

The paper explicitly acknowledges that variance-reduction techniques and 'real applications, e.g. new deep learning optimizer' are left as future work, meaning the main contribution remains largely theoretical without demonstrated impact.
Only diagonal (and rank-1/rank-2) forms of the estimator are empirically explored; the claimed capability to estimate block-diagonal or full-tensor structures is not empirically illustrated at all.

strengths: Rigorous and extensive theoretical development: the paper carefully characterizes the spectrum of the Fisher information metric on the statistical simplex (core space), derives tight rank-1/diagonal envelopes (Lemma 2), and propagates these into deterministic bounds on the full neuromanifold FIM (Proposition 5) with explicit error analysis (Propositions 7-10).

The identification of unbounded coefficient of variation for standard Monte Carlo FIM estimators (Section 4.1) is a clear and well-motivated diagnosis of a real practical problem, elegantly illustrated with a heavy-tailed toy example.

The proposed Hutchinson-based estimator is a genuinely useful practical contribution: it is unbiased, computable with a single backward pass (same cost as computing the gradient of the loss), and provably has bounded coefficient of variation (≤ sqrt(2)), which is a meaningful theoretical guarantee absent from prior deterministic (eFIM) or MC estimators.

Reasonably broad empirical validation across six model/task combinations spanning NLP (DistilBERT, RoBERTa), vision (ResNet-50, EfficientNet-B0), and audio (Wav2Vec2), with ground-truth FIM computed for comparison, lending some external validity to the theoretical claims.
Clear, well-organized exposition of related work situating the contribution relative to eFIM, Kronecker-factored approximations, and existing MC/Hutchinson trace estimator literature.
All lemmas/propositions are proven in detail in the appendix, aiding reproducibility of the theoretical results.
weaknesses: No downstream application is demonstrated; the paper explicitly acknowledges this as a limitation, leaving the practical significance of the tighter bounds and lower-variance estimator largely unvalidated beyond RelMAE tables (e.g., no natural-gradient optimizer, pruning, or continual-learning experiment showing improved outcomes from using F instead of eFIM/MC).

The empirical results in Table 2 are mixed: Hutchinson's estimate is not uniformly best (e.g., on DBpedia and CIFAR-100 the low-rank/diagonal estimators or comparable methods perform similarly or better), somewhat diluting the 'clear win' narrative built up in the main text.

The deterministic bounds (Propositions 5, 7, 8) are mathematically intricate but their practical utility is not clearly demonstrated empirically — no experiment directly evaluates the tightness of these deterministic bounds on real networks, only the numerical estimators (F, F^DG, F^LR) are benchmarked.

The low-rank estimator relies on power iteration or spectral decomposition of a C×C matrix, adding computational overhead that scales with C, with only modest empirical speed comparison (mostly a caveat noted for CIFAR-100 with C=100).

The core theoretical device (Hutchinson trace/vector trick applied to Fisher information via sqrt(p) reweighting) is an incremental combination of known techniques (Hutchinson's estimator, natural gradient/FIM decomposition via chain rule) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea, and this could be more explicitly acknowledged/contrasted against closely related recent work (e.g., Soen & Sun 2024) cited in the paper.
The paper is very dense and proof-heavy, with most technical content deferred to a lengthy appendix; the main text's readability and self-containedness for a general AI audience is limited.
Only diagonal entries of the FIM are empirically evaluated; the claimed extension to off-diagonal entries and the full covariance structure is asserted but not empirically validated.

strengths: The paper develops a rigorous and fairly complete theoretical treatment of the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) for classifier networks, starting from the low-dimensional statistical simplex (core space) and extending bounds to the full neuromanifold via the Gauss-Newton/pullback relationship. All propositions and lemmas are proven in detail in the appendix.

The proposed Hutchinson-based FIM estimator is an elegant and practically appealing contribution: it is unbiased, requires only a single additional backward pass (reusing forward-pass logits), is architecture-agnostic, and has a provably bounded coefficient of variation (CV ≤ √2), in contrast to the Monte Carlo estimator whose CV is shown to be unbounded via a concrete heavy-tailed counterexample.

The empirical study spans a reasonably diverse set of real, large-scale models and modalities (DistilBERT/SST-2, DistilBERT/DBpedia, RoBERTa/MNLI, ResNet-50 and EfficientNet-B0 on CIFAR-100, Wav2Vec2/SpeechCommands), which is more extensive than typical toy validations of such theoretical estimators.

The spectral analysis of the simplex FIM (Theorem 1, Lemma 2) giving tight-ish eigenvalue bounds and best rank-1/diagonal envelopes under the Löwner order is a clean and potentially reusable piece of information-geometric analysis.
The paper is honest about its limitations, explicitly noting that no downstream application (e.g., a new optimizer) is built on top of the proposed estimator.
weaknesses: The practical payoff is thin: the paper itself admits the proposed estimator is not plugged into any downstream pipeline (optimizer, pruning, regularizer), so the claimed 'importance even in the absence of a specific application' is asserted rather than demonstrated with any end-task improvement (e.g., faster/better natural-gradient training, improved pruning decisions).

Only diagonal FIM entries are evaluated empirically, even though the theoretical contributions (Proposition 5, Corollary 6, Propositions 7-10) concern the full matrix and low-rank/diagonal bounds; the deterministic bounds (the core theoretical contribution of Section 3) are never empirically validated for tightness in the neuromanifold setting, only asserted qualitatively ('found through numerical simulations... quite tight') without accompanying numbers or figures.

The relationship to prior closely related work (Soen & Sun 2021, 2024, 'Trade-Offs of diagonal Fisher information matrix estimators') is acknowledged but not clearly differentiated; the paper states its bounds 'improve over existing bounds... of F(θ) [Soen & Sun, 2024]' without a quantitative or structural comparison, making it hard to judge incremental novelty versus that line of work.

Several entries in Table 2 show very large RelMAE for the empirical FIM baseline (53.9, 56.8), which is not sufficiently discussed or sanity-checked; it raises questions about whether the eFIM baseline was implemented/tuned reasonably or whether these are outliers driven by near-zero ground truth values (despite the ε regularization), undermining confidence in the comparison.

The reported accuracy of the main proposed estimator (~20% RelMAE on average) is still fairly large for a method marketed as having 'guaranteed quality,' and no discussion is given of how this error scales with network size, depth, or accumulation of minibatch averaging in realistic training scenarios.

Many of the mathematical tools used (Cauchy interlacing, Gershgorin circle theorem, Von Neumann trace inequality, Hoffman-Wielandt inequality) are standard, and their application, while careful, is fairly mechanical; the overall technical novelty relative to known Hutchinson trace-estimator variance results and known FIM approximation schemes (K-FAC, low-rank/empirical Fisher) seems incremental.

The notation is extremely dense (F, F̄, F̂, 𝔽 and I, Ī, Î, 𝕀 variants, core-space vs neuromanifold superscripts, multiple h-functions), which significantly hampers readability and may limit accessibility and reproducibility for readers not already steeped in this specific notation.

No code release or detailed reproducibility information (hyperparameters for power iteration beyond T=30, batch sampling details, variance of reported metrics across seeds) is provided, making it hard to verify or reproduce the reported RelMAE numbers.

The paper does not compare against other single-backward-pass or low-overhead FIM/Hessian approximations beyond eFIM (e.g., K-FAC-style or other structured approximations), limiting the positioning of the proposed estimator relative to the broader practical toolbox.

strengths: Rigorous, self-contained theoretical development: the paper derives a comprehensive set of deterministic bounds (envelopes, low-rank and diagonal bounds) for the FIM in a low-dimensional 'core' statistical simplex and carefully lifts these results to the high-dimensional neuromanifold via the Gauss-Newton/pullback structure.

The proposed Hutchinson-based FIM estimator is a genuinely useful practical contribution: it is unbiased, provably has bounded coefficient of variation (CV ≤ √2 for Rademacher probes), and can be computed with a single backward pass, in contrast to Monte Carlo estimators that require O(batch size) backward passes.
Good diagnosis of a real failure mode of standard MC estimators (unbounded CV under heavy-tailed input distributions), motivating the need for the proposed estimator.

Broad and diverse empirical validation across six model/task combinations spanning NLP (DistilBERT, RoBERTa), vision (ResNet-50, EfficientNet-B0), and audio (Wav2Vec2), with a sensible RelMAE metric and reasonable ground-truth computation protocol.
Extensive appendix with full proofs for all lemmas/propositions, which supports reproducibility and correctness verification of the theoretical claims.
Clear and honest discussion of when low-rank/diagonal variants are preferable (e.g., fine-tuned models with near low-rank core FIM) versus when the generic Hutchinson estimator dominates.
weaknesses: No downstream application is demonstrated: the paper explicitly acknowledges that the proposed estimator is not plugged into an optimizer, pruning method, or other pipeline that would use FIM estimates, leaving the practical significance of the improved estimator somewhat unproven beyond RelMAE numbers.

The reported RelMAE for the proposed unbiased estimator (~0.2, i.e., ±20% relative error) is still fairly large in absolute terms; the paper does not contextualize whether this level of accuracy is sufficient for practical downstream use (e.g., natural gradient steps or saliency-based pruning).

Empirical comparisons are limited to simple single-backward-pass baselines (empirical FIM, diagonal/low-rank variants); no comparison against more structured approximations such as K-FAC or other established practical FIM/curvature estimators that are widely used in the literature, which limits the ability to judge relative competitiveness.

Only diagonal FIM entries are evaluated empirically; the off-diagonal behavior, which is often more important for understanding curvature/geometry (e.g., in natural gradient descent), is only briefly mentioned as 'readily extendable' but not empirically validated.

The low-rank estimator's computational cost (spectral decomposition or power iteration) is only lightly benchmarked (e.g., a single remark about ~2x slowdown on CIFAR-100); a more systematic scalability/cost analysis across C would strengthen the practical claims.

Some of the core-space theoretical results (e.g., simplex FIM spectrum bounds, rank-1/diagonal envelopes) are somewhat incremental extensions of well-known properties of the categorical Fisher information matrix, and the novelty relative to prior MC information geometry work (Soen & Sun, Nielsen & Hadjeres) could be articulated more sharply.
The paper is very dense with heavy notation and many propositions/lemmas, which may hinder accessibility and adoption by practitioners despite the practical motivation.
